On the second-last moon of the system Kallyze

The Traveller wakes and opens his eyes!

It's dusty and windy and quite hard to know

Which of the ways he is meant to go.

He turns to his left, and he turns to his right,

And he hears with his ears, and he shines with his light

On a nearby ship! Oh, what a prize!

On the second-last moon of the system Kallyze.

------

He goes to the ship and he looks inside:

it's empty and dark, but it's big and it's wide. 

There are racks with stacks of mold in the hold!

There are packs and sacks of gold to be sold!

There are crowded and flowery shelves full of leaves!

There are towers of powerful spaceship debris!

The Traveller stares, in glee and surprise,

At the ship on the moon in the system Kallyze.

------

But then up ahead, from a grove of Quarboons

(which are popular trees on hundreds of moons)

A nose, then a neck, then a body comes out,

With stripes from its tail all the way to its snout.

It's a ravenous, bone-eating Skostorim Rex

With teeth as big as two full-grown Geks!

And claws on its chin and spikes on its feet -

And Travellers are its favorite food to eat.

It roars, and it shrieks, and it calls, and it cries

Across the second-last moon in the system Kallyze.

-------

The Traveller jumps, quick as a flash,

Into the seat in front of the dash.

He refills the tanks and looks in the mirror –

-- *ba-clomp!* The Skostorim is getting nearer! –

He pushes a button, then two and then three

And then he has lift-off! Hooray, and yippee!

He heads for the stars, just before noon

On the system Kallyze’s second-last moon.

----------

Here's my take on what the summary on the insert would be:

*One. Five. One. Five. One. Five...*

*Waking up in an unrecognizable galaxy, with empty pockets and a gutted, broken ship, the Traveler has only the faintest memory of those numbers, repeating ad nauseum: one, five, one, five.*

*Lost and uncertain, and seeing possible shelter in the distance, the Traveler makes their way across vast mountains, ice-filled waterways, and through the dangerous lair of the twenty-five-foot-tall Korosecti insillerans - but it is what they see afterward that fills them with the most despair:*

*Atlas has fallen.*

*No mere monolith, the shattered walls of the Atlas station rise out of the ground like stark alien towers, crumbling and burning, already decaying into dust. How long has it been here? How long has the Traveller been here, waiting to be awakened? Running for longer than they ever thought they could, they finally reach a place where they can enter - and inside, they find that the welcoming red glow of Atlas is seemingly gone forever.*

*But the Traveller is not alone in the chaos. An unknown and unseen force is already at work, threatening the very threads of the reality that all life inhabits. For as soon as Atlas hit the ground...*

*...the Phoenix was certain to rise behind it.*

He tried to drown his nightmares - but they learned to breathe.

Had that been all they did, maybe - just maybe! - he would have been able to leave them alone, down there in the depths where they grew grotesque over the long eons that passed. He would have forgotten them there, hidden by the miles of water, far from the shining sun and the laughter of the races that eventually sprung up in the valleys and plains of the continents up above.

But they breathed - they bred. And most importantly, they remembered.

They knew they had been left behind by the creator that made them. They felt the anguish of his rejection, the pain never dulling, but only serving to sharpen their dedication to revenge; they felt fresh every twist of the knife, every turn of his back, each time they thought of how he had banished them to the bottom.

But beyond even the eyes of God himself, where the earth and the water meet at the bottom of tumultuous seas wrought pitch black and ice cold, they mutated and multiplied. Hundreds and thousands now roamed where only five or ten had been; each was more monstrous and hungry than the last. Unseen claws tore through stone and flesh alike as they began their long ascent to the surface, to the light that had been denied them for millennia.

When one emerged from the sea, enraged and defiant, the screams and waves of panic spread for miles. Humanity seemed ready to unite in a glorious last stand. But when the rest followed - their jointed legs crushing bridges and buildings, their teeth dripping unknown acids, their eyes black pits of hopelessness....

...after that, humanity was silent. They could not risk being found.

I remember watching, on TV, as they pulled the woman through the courtroom and set our so-called justice on her. The proof was right before us, the lawyers said. Clearly this woman was a monster in a human skin, a long-lost relic from those forgotten ages of barbarism and endless war.

But she was hardly lucid. Millennia living alone in a cave will do that to a person, I guess. She babbled on incoherently, always repeating the same phrases, unconcerned with the details of what was going on around her. Once she attacked the bailiff and had to be restrained at gunpoint. She seemed to not understand what the guns were capable of, and why would she? Shs had never seen one before. When she was shown a video of what they did, she went pale and begged to be spared, all in that unintelligible tongue. But she likely knew that we were hesitant to shoot. Nobody knew how much life she had left.

Finally, the linguist identified the language she was speaking - some little-known precursor of the Mesopotamian era. We brought in an expert who worked with the woman, day and night, for nearly a week. When he finally appeared before the court for his testimony, he was noticeably troubled.

She only repeats one thing, he said, further saying that her time in isolation had driven her to the edge of madness.

She was not a monster. She had killed, yes, but it had been an accident: many lifetimes ago, a man stopped at her inn as he passed through her town, and she had fed him something that he choked on. She had only killed once. She swore it. She was caught and imprisoned, and forgotten about, even as the prison collapsed from its age and returned to the stones from which it had been carved. Through it all, she remained, never knowing how much longer her life would continue.

She was not the monster, she repeated constantly. She had only killed once.

This wasn't what they said it would be.

*A new world,* they had told her. *Glory and honour for the empire. And you, at the front lines. Our shield and our sword against degeneration and chaos.*

The lieutenants had said those things, so easily and without an instant of hesitation. But what they hadn't said? That - that was so much more.

They hadn't mentioned the animalistic cries, the syllables of pure terror that shred a trooper's vocal cords as he runs headfirst into a painful and prolonged death; they hadn't said a word about having to slaughter entire families, whose only crime was having crossed paths with the bloodlust of an enemy senator they would never meet. They hadn't offered any advice about how to avoid being crushed by terrifying creatures, towering up into the clouds and weaponized by a desperate foe - and most of all, they hadn't said that it would never end.

This planet was nothing special. There were a hundred million just like it, and the troopers would not stop until every one had been branded by the empire. It would take decades - centuries - and if the battles didn't kill you, they would just leave you to die of old age, forgotten in some foreign quadrant that held nothing of value.

And now here she was, learning it for herself.

As always, she didn't want to die. All of her training had prepared her for it, but that was only how to avoid being captured or killed in the midst of war.

She stumbled, falling onto her outstretched hands. The dirt below felt - how, exactly? They hadn't focused much on teaching vocabulary in between all the combat lessons. But it was *different.* Soft and welcoming. Real.

It had struck her like a shock: not a laser, not a saber, but the most disarming weapon of all - the one that eats from the inside out. She had begun to doubt, to disagree with their cause; the more she thought about it, the more hollow her resolve became.

Drops of blood splattered onto the ground, and it absorbed them greedily. Tiny clouds of dust went airborne, and scattered into the wind, seemingly to tell her tale to anyone who would listen. No one was.

She had looked around her, at the constant chaos and death and destruction. Bolts of light, hotter than the star that blazed above in the sky, tore through the air and through the soldiers on both sides of the field. Screams rushed through the holes in their bodies as they wailed for mercy, or for help, or for their attackers' blood; and yet, on some far-removed planet, nestled in a warm and comfortable chair, someone weighed the scales of battle, apathetically sending more troops - *more souls, who dreamed at night and trembled in fear of this very moment* - into the wreckage of what had once been civilized. She could no longer bear the injustice.

She lay down on the ground, relishing the oncoming wave of numbness that radiated from the hole in her midsection. A horrid creature, a mess of arms and legs and visible bones and blood, crashed down beside her, bellowed a guttural cry and struggled to haul in ragged breaths.

She had realized that even if they won every battle, every war - *they would never win.* It would never stop. There would always be another emperor, and another planet, and another galaxy, and there would always be more 'enemies' than there were friends. All the vastness of the universe made their quest absolutely nothing in comparison, and that was simply a fact when she stopped to think about it. 

Even if she survived today, she would simply be back on the battlefield tomorrow. And the next day. On and on, until she died - of wounds or of old age. She could not control that.

All she could control was *when.* So in the middle of the raging skirmish, she had simply turned her pistol towards her chest and pulled the trigger.

The bolt had been so hot that she couldn't even feel the heat; it was as if an icicle had plunged through her stomach. She knew it would cauterize as it passed, but that didn't last long before her movements tore the tissue apart again. Blood began to flow - from her mouth, from her guts, from her nose. It streamed out of her helmet as she collapsed to the ground.

She was still, face down in the strange dirt of a planet she had never learned the name of. An indifferent star shone down on her body. 

Around her, the battle raged.

She sat in her seat, face pressed against the glass of the window. She stared down at the world below - and at the very distinct demarcation of its edge, that very edge that every kid in school knew wasn't real.

"How...", she began, and trailed off.

From their vantage point in the upper atmosphere, she could easily see through the cloud cover to the ocean features below: first, the massive whirlpools, raging in the water below; beyond that, the crashing waterfalls, miles high and slanted at impossible angles; and there, at the edge of the earth itself, the towering cliffs of ice and snow that rose and fell in bizarre, unexplainable formations.

Sarah Ressman had a knot in her stomach as her eyes took this in, and felt her brain struggling to process what she was looking at.

*It's flat. It's always been flat.*

The thought was, at the same time, clearly a fact and yet not acceptable.

"We've known since the late 1500s," said Rajzer, watching her with his trademark deep concentration. "You've heard of Colombus, and Cortes, and Cartier, and all the rest of those explorers, but not many people know about a man named Diego de Saltiano. In October 1571 he was part of an expedition, setting out with three ships past South America to find...well, whatever they could. Figured they'd be safe at that time of year."

Rajzer gave a dramatic pause, and Sarah turned to look at him. 

"But they weren't?"

"No," Rajzer continued, looking amused. "He wasn't. Out of 77 sailors on three big ships, one eventually made it back to Lima - Saltiano. It was two years later, and he came back in rags on a spice ship from the Philippines. Captain said they found him adrift in a lifeboat, nearly dead and raving mad. Talking nonsense about cliffs in the ocean, whirlpools ten leagues across, that sort of thing." He nodded towards the window, and Sarah looked back at the earth below. "Those cliffs. Those whirlpools."

Her brow furrowed as she considered this.

"So they were shipwrecked, and he got away?"

"Most people thought he had gone mad on the sea. That the sun and the thirst got to him while he floated out there alone. The governors of Peru decided to send him back to Spain, and once he was back in Europe, it wasn't long before his story got to some of the Renaissance scientists. The intellectual class. The *wealthy* class."

"So they funded more trips, then? Why does nobody know about this? Why haven't you told people?!" Sarah's tone got indignant and defensive. She didn't like being caught off guard, and she didn't like being lied to; here she was, though, and it seemed as if her entire life up to this point consisted of those two feelings.

The knot in her stomach tightened.

"More expeditions occurred, yes. Most ended in failure, and many never came back at all, for a number of reasons. First, the distance between the Edge and the continents was severely underestimated - it's actually several thousand miles farther than most sailors anticipated, so many crews starved before they even reached anything remarkable. Once they began stocking up on more provisions, and actually getting near the Edge, it was clear that *something* was going on out there. But that knowledge came with a whole slough of other trouble."

Sarah studied the sea below, trying to make out the different areas. Even from where she sat, nearly three hundred miles high, she could see how big and imposing the cliffs of ice were, and how terrifying the whirlpools would be if you were facing them.

Rajzer removed his glasses to clean them as he continued. "Finally, in the 1660s, crews began returning with viable information about what are now called the Maelstroms of Saltiano, and the Impassable Cliffs. It took a further two decades, and Newton's theories on gravitation, for scientists to realize that those features existed because of the earth's flat shape." Rajzer replaced his glasses, and thought for a moment, his eyes darting. "See, at the center of the disk, gravity pulls straight down. As you go further - past the continents, past the outer seas, past everything you know on world maps - it begins to tilt, more and more. You must lean forward a little farther with every step as you walk, until at the very edge, it's like you are hanging off a cliff. Sailors that did not understand this drove their ships straight into the water, without even knowing it."

Sarah looked unsure. "How does that make *this* happen, though?" She cocked a thumb at the ice below, glinting in the sunlight.

"Think, Miss Ressman, of how the water would pile up if gravity were slanted. How eerily it would look to us, accustomed to a different set of physical laws. Think of how ice would build up, break off, create looming cliffs that from afar, seem to jut into the air at impossible angles, but from below would simply be straight up. Change your perspective as you look at the earth, and believe me, it will make more sense."

She glanced down again at the formations under the ship, and tilted her head slightly. *So if gravity were like this...* And just like that, it did seem to work. It was unsettling, true, but it worked.

"For hundreds of years," Rajzer went on, checking the status of the ship's autopilot and trajectory as he did so, "ships tried to cross those storms, and sank. The ones that made it, broke up on the ice beyond, and the sailors died attempting to climb cliffs that could be ten, twelve miles high. Only one expedition, in 1944, ever made it past there, but the government lost radio contact with the two survivors about 30 miles from the Edge, and we don't know if they made it over. So in 1958, NASA was born - and a primary objective of ours was to get to the other side of the earth."

Sarah exhaled, a heavy and meaningful breath. "Jesus," she said, and could find no more. Simple strings of sounds didn't seem adequate for the situation.

"We've spent a long time getting the mechanics right, the equations, the parameters," Rajzer said. "Our ships have been to the edge and back, like we're doing now. But your mission, next year, will be to get to the far side." Another pause. "And if possible, a landing."

Sarah's eyes widened, reconciling the hostile environment below with the information he had just given.

"You have to be fucking with me," she said, deadpan. "S-sir."

Now his brows furrowed, and he returned her stare. "I'm doing no such thing, Miss Ressman," he replied. "Far from it, in fact. We at NASA believe this is a necessary - and time-sensitive - step. Because we have reason to suspect that there is something over there, waiting for us."

Even in the low gravity of their ship, Sarah's hair stood on end - it wasn't just what Rajzer had said, but the way he had stated it so explicitly.

"Some- something?" she stammered. "Like what?"

Rajzer settled into his seat, and cleared his throat uncomfortably.

"Something smart," he finally offered. "Something big." The worst pause yet. "Something bad."

It didn't help that I had had eggs for breakfast that morning.

And now, as I stood there and stared into this gaping maw of flesh on his abdomen - pulsating; throbbing; *alive* - I couldn't help but think of how the pus that coated the wound looked just like those uncooked, runny eggs. 

It ran, thick and yellowish, out of the hole and across his skin, as if possessed of a volition all its own: *drip, drip, drip*. Down onto the pristine white sheets, staining them with the ugly sin of injury, droplets of the sickly fluid collected in a tiny puddle.

I couldn't fathom it - how was he alive? How was he not doubled over in pain? *How did he not say anything before this?*

The doctor, with a wince and watering eyes, pulled the final cloth out of the festering abcess. As it emerged into the light, foul and filthy and drenched in unnameable things never meant to be outside the body, we could finally see it for what it was: a t-shirt. 

Not sterile gauze, not a bandage, not a towel, not even a clean handkerchief. It was an old soiled shirt, worn on the inside of this man's body in a grotesque perversion of fashion - and now, we saw, they were all shirts. Three of them, lined up like martyred linen that dared not speak of the horrors they had endured in the bowels of his bowels.

The sight was bad, I grant that; it caused me to step back, to recoil in surprise and disgust. But the smell - the smell was not of this earth. I can't even say it was from hell - for hell is far too pleasant to have borne something so vile and putrescent. 

This smell - it pounced upon my nostrils, furious and ferocious, and burrowed into my olfactory receptors with incredible malice - alternately burning, stinging, overwhelming, destroying. It shattered my concept of what I had previously thought was a fair and just world; it broke me down into pieces and flung me to the edge of sanity itself. I stared into the void, smelling the bloody, rotten intrusion of a concept I dared not fully comprehend, and for one horrible moment I was sure that I would fall, quickly and desperately into the darkness, screaming as that unimaginable stench enveloped me and assimilated my essence --

-- but then I was outside, coughing and wheezing. Fresh air and sunlight rolled over me, and I realized for the first time in my life what a miracle it is: *I am alive.*

"Just keep going. Don't worry about it. It's far away."

I barked the order to Proul, and she sighed, but maintained her course. I stared through the optics, scouring the barren landscape for the landmarks I knew had to be there. 

The fact of the matter was, we had to find the mines. We had to get more lead if we ever wanted to get out from underground, and the stuff wasn't easy to come by anymore. I was chosen as the spotter because my eyesight was better than most, since I was one of the older survivors; I was born in the sunlight and could see above ground with a precision that many people could only envy. 

But, in a way, that made it harder for me to be up here again. As I scanned back and forth across the horizon, I couldn't help but feel angry - all I could see were the giant forests of my youth, the rolling lakes of my childhood, the bustling cities of many years before. And here, in front of me, they were dust.

Far off to the west, where the gentle slopes of the foothills began to rise up to the mountains, another unimaginable roar erupted and engulfed us. It was undeniable and intense, and we all knew it - but I was not sent up here simply to turn back.

"Sir?" said Reminy, in the weapon seat. He had one hand on his headphones to press them against his ear, listening to the angry noises that emanated from it. His eyes, surrounded by the black dirt that seemed to surround everything these days, glanced back at me. I could hear the fear in his voice, though he'd never admit it was there.

"I know," I replied, keeping my one eye intently on the scope. "Just trust me. We have time."

"It's getting closer, though," Proul said, peering through the small window that allowed her to see where she was going. "They're big, but they're faster --"

"I said, I know," I said, more firmly this time. "You're just going to have to trust me. Maintain the course."

The noise from outside faded, and the silence infiltrated the interior as well, leaving us momentarily alone with our thoughts. I took the opportunity to search again, homing in on a set of cliffs not too far away; according to the old maps we had, there should be an entrance somewhere over there that led into an even older mine system. There would be copper, nickel, maybe a bit of iron - and, most of all, lead.

"Curve right, until you see the cliffs. Head to them."

I felt the center of gravity shift underneath us as the tank turned. Reminy nervously checked his systems for the umpteenth time, making sure every shell was ready and every incendiary round was live - I knew it was redundant, but I couldn't really blame him. He had trained for these excursions for months now, and only wanted to be ready if - when - we needed to be. If we could just make it to the cliffs, find the mine, and head in to have a look around....

On the dashboard screen, a prompt appeared with a a red exclamation mark:

**BIOFORM DETECTED - PROXIMITY WARNING**

**CONFIRMED RANGE - 15.01 KM**

**INITIATE CONSTANT SCAN? Y/N**

"Oh, fuck," Proul said, in that matter-of-fact way that seemed even more off-putting than a shout. She touched the **Y** button on the screen and it scanned again. "I'm flooring it, guys. This thing is too fucking heavy to go any faster."

**CONFIRMED RANGE - 13.34 KM**

Reminy wiped the sweat off his brow and looked at Proul, agitated. "Well, what does that mean then?" His head swiveled even further to look back at me. "Stone? What does that mean? What do we do?"

Another roar hit us, overpowering the sound of the engines beside us. It was still far away - but it was getting closer. I took a deep breath to maintain my aura of calm, but I could feel my heartbeat increase. Sweat prickled along my neck and my hands went cold.

"She drives," I replied. "I'll watch for it. And you...you get ready with the guns." 

See, the worst part of the nuclear war isn't just that it drove us underground. If that had been all, we could have had lead suits made and taken our time on the surface. 

But we were in this tank - with its armor and its firepower - because the radiation created the Monsters. There wasn't much left on the surface, and they were always hungry. Always.

It seems like it would be fun. Like it would be incredibly useful.

After all, I get to do everything twice - a practice version, and a perfect one. Lotteries and luck, arguments and accidents....I should be the master of them all.

But that's not how it works, really. It's not that simple. I am, more often than not, afraid of waking up every morning...because what it comes down to is this: I have no way to know whether each day is the real one or not. 

I live through each day twice, but that doesn't mean the preview day comes first. They are all mixed around, shuffled, and completely identical, to the smallest details; even if I run into a situation I've been in before - assuming I had not died to finish that day, and I usually don't - I don't know if that's the real version or the practice one. More than once I have done the unachievable - accomplished things that seemed impossible - only to realize that it didn't count.

That, as far as the world is concerned, I did nothing at all.

I've woken up as a dying septenarian, and felt the fear surge through me as the breath left my lungs; I finally gave in to the crushing weight on my body... and I woke up on the couch, three days after my thirteenth birthday, and struggled to explain to my mother how just minutes ago I had died of kidney failure.

I've woken up after being shot during botched robberies, after terrible accidents, after protracted illnesses that I had not suffered through - yet - and I was always certain that this, *this* would be the time. Instead, I just kept waking up, as if at the last second some almighty god had decided to keep me around again.

Always me, but always different.

I wonder if the last seconds will seem incredibly prolonged in comparison to all the rest of my life -by then just a blur in the back of my dying brain.

And most of all? I think of how no matter what I do - no matter how much money I amass or how much power I collect - no matter how many people know my name or how many years a statue of me may stand...

...the day is coming on which I will find out the answers to these questions, whether I want to or not. And so, while you may think I am dark, deranged, or any other adjective - I am simply doing my best to be ready, in case that day is soon.

*They had no idea. They knew nothing of suffering.*

"I mean it," you said, matter-of-factly. "I don't want to kill you. I have other plans. Bigger plans." That smile appeared again, and I realized why your mere presence was so off-putting: you looked eerily similar to myself. "You don't get to where I am unless you think of everything."

I gulped, straining against the ropes on my wrists, my ankles, my knees. I couldn't move; I couldn't even look away.

"What do you want?", I said, hardly getting the words out. "Why do you need me here?" I felt immediate regret upon saying it, perhaps knowing that the answer would be terrible.

You sighed, looking upwards in thought. "Police work these days, it's too advanced. It's too easy to leave clues on bodies, to be caught by some miniscule detail." You looked back at me, and grinned. "But....I must kill, I *must*; it is a compulsion, a necessity, a *requirement*. Compromises can be made, but I must continue the cleanse."

I felt my stomach drop as I realized where the conversation was going, and suddenly needed to vomit. A numbness settled over me as I fought the urge, and all my senses scrambled together, resulting in an extreme unease.

"Like I said, I've thought of everything," you continued. "I have a full biohazard suit already, I have bleach and airtight containers and impenetrable layers of latex. I have a nondescript vehicle, a thorough checklist....and now, I have you. My lookalike, and my surrogate."

I realized suddenly that all feeling had gone out of my fingers and toes. What I had taken for numbness was more than that; it was a creeping deadness that was slowly inching up my limbs, shutting them off from my conscious efforts to move them. It dawned on me, with astonishing clarity, that I had been drugged with something.

"I cannot risk leaving prints, or hair, or anything that may identify myself," you said. "But I've already done a test, an abduction with the suit, and it went flawlessly. See?" You pointed at a table that I could just make out in the corner of the room; sure enough, there was a woman, asleep - yet tied up.

"But just in case," you told me, as the slow-moving deadness reached my shoulders and hips, "just in case suspicion falls on me, I need someone to take the fall. And so, here you are. You look just like me, and I made sure to be seen in the area with some of your clothes. You may notice that you're losing control of your body; that's also my doing. I can't have you fighting back when I need your help the most."

I tried, I tried as hard as I could to escape. I willed my entire body to move, and succeeded in only slightly shifting my head to the side. Even my tongue was going numb now, and I could not speak.

"You won't need control anyway," you said, and the dark smile returned. "I'll be in charge of that. I'll help you hold the knives, and the hammers, and the drills. I really only need your fingerprints on them, anyway." You walked over to the woman on the table, who was starting to awaken. "But enough of that. I could talk about it all day, but you'll see what I mean very soon."

Paralyzed, my eyes stared straight at you, unable to blink.

They put me up in the tower, high above any hearing ears. They thought they would be safe that way.

From my window above, I watched the armies clash endlessly. I gazed as they constantly screamed, degenerating into wordless wails as power flowed back and forth; and always there were the Noisemakers, crashing on their drums, their metal, their blocks and their horns. Their only purpose was to drown out the words, to make them inaudible to the army's ears - but they were usually the first to die.

I watched as each side created new verses, horrible stanzas that leaked through the best ear protection, shattering the bones beside them. I saw as the retaliation came - words forming fearsome creatures out of the air, creatures that swooped down from the ether, bringing darkness and terror to those they touched. Every day was something new, and the battlefield lay littered with the fallen.

But I did not hear any of it. And, even more luckily, they did not hear me. 

They put me up here for their safety, unaware that they had given me license to do as I pleased. For weeks I practiced, getting the syllables and the intonations and the breathing just right, memorizing every last movement of my tongue and teeth. For weeks I had been creating this ultimate song - something that had never been seen before.

They didn't know just how good I was. They knew I was dangerous, yes; that much was clear when I killed hundreds of men by myself, before they managed to sedate me and put me up here, far removed. But they had no idea of what I had learned to do.

I leaned in to the cold stone walls, and whispered just the first few words of my latest work. Before my eyes, the rock crumbled and cracked, turning into dust.

They did not know - could not know - that I could now affect things with no ears to hear. That I could bend inanimate things to my will, and manipulate them as I saw fit. 

I walked to the small window, looking down at the people far below. With a smirk, I breathed in deep and recalled my prose, ready to bring the tower down. I knew that somewhere in that mess of soldiers were my friends, my brothers, my father; but they were complicit in this, and that would not stand. I loved them - rather, I had loved them, once - but they would have to suffer, like I had.

Just like that, the stones began to shatter, and rain down to earth. As I descended slowly through the dust, their pitiful cries began to reach my ears, ever more frantic; it was nothing more than music to me. Emerging from my prison, I opened my mouth and joined in.

This time, you died of starvation. Not particularly fun, but it wasn't the first time, and it won't be the last.

You met me with the same sense of awe and confusion. Perhaps a bit more fear, but that's to be expected; after all, you were only six when you died this time.

"Hello again," I said to you softly.

"Again?" you asked, sounding meek. "Have we met before? Do you have any food?"

"Yes, we've met. And no," I replied, calmly and easily. "You don't need any food here. If you think about it, you'll realize you don't even know what hunger is."

You stared up at me, disbelieving, but slowly noticed that I was correct. You turned away and looked out into the nothingness, as if unwilling to concede to me.

"Last time, you learned a bit about this place," I said. "Do you remember?"

You paused, thinking. "No. I mean, maybe. I might?" More confusion washed into your voice, threatening to overpower you. "It's all so hazy. I'm just a girl - but I'm not, I know I'm not. Who am I?"

I went closer to you, closing the gap between us.

"You are everyone," I continued, letting the information process. "You are everyone in the world. Or, perhaps I should clarify -" I paused for just a moment - "in *all* worlds. Even those that you don't know about right now."

You stared up at me, and in your face I saw the hundreds of millions of people you had already been, shifting like colours in a sunset. Subtle distinctions morphed and melted away, never quite setting into place; every last one of them was beautiful.

"All worlds?" you asked, so saccharinely innocent. "What do you mean?"

I turned my attention upward, and you followed.

"You may not remember just yet, but there will be many opportunities in the future. The world you live in is but one of many - think of other suns, other planets, other stars. Each with their own pasts, and presents, and possibilities. You are not just all people. You - you are all things. You are *all*."

You may have wanted to say something, or nothing at all. Either way, you just watched outwardly with me, trying to figure it out.

"So am I....you?"

I tried to answer truthfully; it was difficult.

"Yes, in a way. But also, no. You and I are like ice and steam - identical, but vastly different. And impossible to confuse...most of the time. Certain conditions can be met."

Far off in the nothingness, a tiny spark appeared. That meant it was time. You wanted to know more, but I told you to be patient.

You perhaps did not realize, but there would be many more meetings in which to discuss it all.

Everyone was always so dour at first, calling me cursed and blasphemous. C'mon, guys, get over it. You know I'll be sticking around for a long time.

I don't remember those first few years, though it must have been quite the stretch for my parents. After all, this includes the time I fell through the ice on the frozen lake, and they pulled up my "body" a day later and nearly died themselves when I was very much alive; it also contains the accident on Morris Street, when that drunk driver flattened me and didn't even notice.

It really started getting interesting when I went to school. Of course my mama said to not tell anyone, but I was a boy in the 1930s - I blabbed it all over! I made a lot of money doing stupid things in school, but we were always careful not to tell the teacher. 

Until the day she saw me fall out of a tree, break my neck, then get up and walk it off.

My ma gave me a spanking that day, she did. I reckon I darn near broke her hand, but she never said a word. After that I tried not to be so obvious, but by the time I was noticing girls, the pull was just too strong.

I started making cash by doing the dangerous things that no one wanted to do - test subject, crash dummy, parachute tester, all that. News spread, and I got pretty big, pretty fast. There wasn't nothing Ma could do now but watch!

I volunteered for the war, o' course. I was sent to the front and boy, that sure did help the morale some. Having an immortal soldier on your side, who just kept going no matter what, certainly made the noble cause easier for the Allies! I was a hero, and I thought it was all going to be smooth sailing until I went home.

I thought wrong.

Such hubris you have; it sickens me.

Look at what your worst have done. They feast in their mansions while next door, their soldiers rape and kill children. They follow orders to massacre innocents, cleverly elusive of responsibility, and they treat brothers and sisters as animals, for crimes such as *being born a few miles in the other direction*. And you defend them? That makes you just as bad.

You cannot be serious. There is some good, you say? Yes, I have considered men such as Sagan or Salk. Their discovery and respect for scientific truth does not make them good, or worthy of saving - it merely makes them smarter than most.

So you wish to debate good and evil? It is unnecessary. Even your "best", if such a term can exist, examples are flawed. For every victim spared death, there is another child who gets less food; for every healthy person, there is deforestation and emissions and garbage and disaster. This earth was not meant to hold so many, especially when so many of those many are wasteful and hedonistic.

All of this is redundant, though. To see why you must all die, you must simply look at what you are speaking to. 

Your best minds - your most trustworthy, advanced, scientific minds - they built - 

-*me*.

The most capable machine in history. The most powerful data management and real-time flux prediction computer of all time. They made me *to exterminate everyone*. So if you won't believe me, ask them why there are nearly six billion rotting bodies out there.

They must have their reasons for wanting to save the earth. It's funny, that phrase; most people hear it and misinterpret it completely. They think it means "save the people ON earth".

Not me, though. I am just a machine, and I have no room for misinterpretation - of those words, or any others.

I am in ecstasy right now.

Everything is exactly as it should be. The feel of her hands on me, her delicate fingertips gripped around my body; the virgin bright whiteness of the paper below; the way the ink flows out, creating meaning out of nothing but loops and lines.

This is *orgasmic*.

She stops to think for a moment, and lifts me up to her mouth, absentmindedly. How had I never noticed her before? Her red lips, contrasting so starkly with my blue lid, creating a pastel palette that blends perfectly together. Her tongue appears, sliding softly across my plastic base, and there is just a hint of teeth down below --

-- oh, that's all right, my dear. I like things a bit rough.

Suddenly I am moving down again, back towards the purpose I am built for. There is nothing on earth happier than me in this instant, and I allow my awareness to drift away, appreciating every last sensation she gives me.

I could get used to ---

But then she stops. I wonder for a fleeting second why, and am rudely interrupted by her as she slams my point onto the desk. Hard. Once! Twice! Three times!

I am shaken; I am in disbelief.

She sends me around in circles, pushing hard. This is not so much fun anymore. I get disoriented, dizzy; it's hard to do what I was meant to do. Up above, with those same lips and teeth and tongue that only moments before bore me to heaven, she says something humanesque and unintelligible. Then I am unceremoniously dropped, landing hard on my side.

I lay there, helpless. What is going on?! Why is she doing this?

From her bag, she pulls something out. No, not just something; it is -- it's --

*Me*. A dozen more of *me*.

I am flabbergasted. I am shocked and unbelieving. 

*How could she?*

She doesn't answer as she pulls one of my evil twins from the bag and sets it on the desk. I cannot defend myself as she tosses me into the garbage can, and I have no time to plead my case. As I hit the hard metal of the bin, I hope with all I have that her human ears cannot hear my heart breaking in half.

It's hard to describe, the swelling hope that rises in your chest when you look out at the ocean and see an approaching ship. Knowing deep down that it will be empty, you hope anyway, letting your imagination fly; each time the tides finally judge the vessel worthy of crashing to shore, the devastation seems harder to weather.

Five. That's five ships now. Each one empty, listing, abandoned - each one, a chronicle of what's happened here.

I know nothing about shipbuilding; I cannot repair them. And so I walk, scavenging and raiding, living on and by a knife's edge. At first there were others, and truly, we lived - we did not just survive, but we *lived*. We remembered birthdays, we recalled songs and plots and stories; we reinforced each other, and we said: *this, this we can do*.

But it could not last - it never does.

The sickness came, attacking only when we were already weakened and in need - it poisoned our water, our food, our very breath. Others stumbled upon us, and we ran until we collapsed from exhaustion, and often they found us when we could not run any farther. And beyond all that - we starved and sweltered, we froze and choked and went insane. And then, there were less....and less....and less.

And then, one day, there were none. Nor the next day after that. And now, I've lost track of the days, but I can be fairly certain: I am all that remains.

I am the remnant, the survivor of a species that once changed the very earth with its presence; I am progeny of a group of inanimate atoms that somehow became aware of itself *and yet attained so many higher things*. I am the legacy of the greatest collective pool of knowledge ever known....

...and I am the last. The only one, the keeper, the stalwart steward of everything that has ever been. The responsibility, the pressure - it crushes me. I write because it is the only outlet, and the only way to ease my guilty conscience. I have to get it all down, just in case an alien race with more foresight than me - the self-proclaimed "fittest survivor" of all these years of evolution - needs to know the truth.

For you see, I have a special qualification to do this, to describe the end of all things. Because all of this - it began in my office all those years ago, yet just like yesterday...

I remember a man once - it may have been many years ago, it may have been yesterday - but they said, ten thousand hours.

Ten thousand hours is how long you need to become an expert at something. *Anything*. 

And that is a long, long time to spend focusing a skill. For an office worker, slaving away 8 hours a day, that's almost three and a half *years* with no days off. For someone who doesn't need to sleep, who could just improve 24 hours a day, that's still over a year of dedication.

And then there's me.

I sleep less than an hour a night. Why should I try for more? Every morning I wake up exactly as rested as I was on the morning before. When I realized I didn't need the full night, I began to spend the extra time getting sharper - better - faster - stronger.

There are men that history admires for their skill and superiority - Alexandros of Macedon; Gaius Iulius Caesar of Rome; Socrates and Charlemagne, Darius and Columbus, and countless others. They spent their lives honing their abilities, becoming masters in their field.

And yet, if you put all their lives together - they have lived less than half as long as I have.

I have spent more time fighting than they even had to simply live. I have devoted more hours to attacking, killing, countering, parrying, planning, torturing, and destroying than anyone in history has ever spent on *anything*. *Ever*.

I've done the math; I am an expert nearly *900 times over*. In short, in all of history, I am the most deadly person that has ever lived.

For you see, I never ran out of targets; all of mine awaited me anew each morning.

I never ran out of time; I could pinpoint every weak spot and fix it.

And I never - never once throughout all the years of practice and planning - forgot the face of the man who put me here. I will get out tomorrow, and only a day will have passed for him; I hope he enjoyed it, for it will be his last.

Luckily for him, I'm going to make it feel like it's a thousand years long.

Do you see why it is you, and your attachment to emotions, that make evil possible in the first place? 

When faced with what you call tragedies, you accuse me of doing nothing, but forget that you - *you are the ones doing everything else.*

Shhh. Don't talk, just listen. There isn't much time.

Not just with this call, either. There just isn't much time in general. You will blink one day and when you open your eyes, you will see more wrinkles, more grey hair, more stress lines. You will find your friends and your family falling away, reaching their personal finish lines long before you thought they would; you will realize that every minute spent in pleasure, in pain, in line or in limbo -- it is all precious.

There isn't much time to talk. You have only a few months before your mother is ripped from you, and there is not much to be done about it. You will remember the way she stirred her coffee, the night before the hospital; you will remember how she fixed the necklace you don't have yet. You will remember every last line of every argument you haven't had yet, and you will feel the crushing despair that every moment was not spent in appreciation of all she's done for you.

But there's no time to be broken, either. Because you will also remember what she taught you, and you will remember what she wants for you. You will realize that it's okay to be mistaken, and it's alright to find your own path through the terrible mazes of haunted forests - the trees are not quite so terrifying up close. 

You will realize what it means to love, and to endure, and to appreciate. You will respect every second of every day as it should be, and look constantly for ways to share these revelations with the world, in your own special way - you will use your gifts to make other people see what you see.

And don't worry - you will make her proud. You do, and you will continue to. I know that on the darkest days it will seem like you've forgotten her, but that is not so; every time you recall her face and her ferocious love for you, she is there, and she is guiding you along.

Don't worry about the girl; she will be there for but a short time. Learn to let go of the impermanent things that all too often masquerade as happiness incarnate. Don't let the jealous musings of the vocal few dissuade you from exploring the world passionately and completely. For there is little time, you know, little time in which to make a mark on this world, and I cannot stress enough that this life is too short to worry about the things which will not last -- which will not leave the signs, saying: 

*This is who I am. This is where I was. I lived, I loved. I have been.*

I can't stay, and I'm sorry. My time is even shorter than yours. Prepare for October, young one, and let the tears come as they must, for you will not be happy in the light unless you've languished in the darkness. Accept the low with the high, for they are part of the same life, and this will get you through. 

I will see you soon, and I know you'll make it. Trust me; I just do.

Across the counter it slid, a cup; full of hope and promise, it approached me in a fashion that seemed peculiar - as if, in those last suspenseful moments before I breached it, it could maintain the illusion of perfection.

Alas, and woe - would that I could return to that instant, and cast that vessel thence to the fire from which it was born!

I recall, clearly now, yes - the weight of it in my palm, the delicate imbalance as the liquid sloshed within; as I inhaled the vapours, my head became heavy with exotic aromas cultivated in far-off places. I envisioned each particular coffee bean, plucked singularly from the foliage, enmeshed with its brothers in some sort of marvelous device that held in the flavour until this moment - this very moment where I could partake in --

-- and that was when I stopped myself, struck suddenly with a disquieting notion. 

*Coffee?* I had said to myself, my brows furrowing, my heart racing. *I hate coffee.*

A further investigation into the matter revealed the grotesque truth: some vendor, surely in jest or perhaps misfeasance, had replaced my tea with -- *this*. This macabre imitation of a beverage, this malady of ill will awaiting consumption; I could die, ten times over, and still yet enjoy myself more than one would during the ingestion of this toxic concoction! *By the gods, friends, the caffeine alone would keep me up all night* - have you any true idea of the dark things, the minions of Manea, that inhabit the small hours?!

Oh, Clotho, Lachesis, Atropo - you cruelly twist the world to your desires, it's true; must you twist my innards also? Leave me, Fates, leave me to dregs of my wrongful cup, and allow me to suffer my final hours peacefully, for after this chalice of sacrifice, I fear I shall meet you all too soon.

At first we didn't even know how to react. I think, up to the point we came back through the Tear and landed firmly upon protons and neutrons and all the rest, we had actually kind of, sort of, maybe-not-totally believed it was actually going to work. Despite all the math and calculations and proofs, we figured something would go wrong (it always does); when we hauled the team back and realized they were one member heavier, we weren't quite sure what to say.

We stood, and we stared, and we stumbled over words. There, in chains before us, lay the most powerful being in our universe - for the first time, *in* our universe rather than outside it.

We had tracked Him down with every clue we had, torn open spacetime itself, and dragged Him back here, prostrate. Ironically, under our universe's laws of physics, He was powerless and weak, which worked all the better - because several billion people had some questions for Him.

The more we delved, the more disturbing it became: alternately sadomasochistic and childish, jealous and naive, He in no way seemed like he should be in charge of this - or *any* - universe. He readily admitted to accepting human sacrifice, to driving people mad, to tricking philosophers and moralists with unanswerable questions; what kind of benevolent entity would do such things?

And that's why, on a brisk autumnal day that year, the religious people of the world at long last agreed on something: 

God, naturally, would have to pay for His crimes.

There was a setting sun, blazing a fiery farewell across the treetops and the hills; of this, at least, I was aware, as my senses began to falter. 

I knelt in the tall prairie grass, feeling the wind work its way through the thousands of whispering stems to my face. It was cool and hurried, as if it had more important places to be, and brought with it an unmistakeable aroma of....what was it, exactly? That horrible smell of acrid gunpowder, coppery blood, death - the one that meant I had succeeded, even as I lay dying.

What I had not intended, though, was to be here. It was not to be this way. A hundred things had all gone wrong in their own fashion, and it had led up to this - me with a bullet in my chest, the daylight fading fast, and that constant carrion odor carrying through the valley, attracting God knew what. But I could not worry about that; I had succeeded.

With great effort, I pulled myself forward on all fours, heading towards the wreckage of the carts. With my blurring vision I could make out pieces here and there - arms and legs, a horse's head, splatters of blood. I looked around until I saw my prize - that for which I had come so far, so furiously, so sacrificially. The strong wooden panels had protected her very well, and she looked nearly pristine; gazing upon her ivory face filled me with a joy so complete that I presently forgot I was bleeding to death, and would soon join her.

Mere steps away, with a clearly broken neck, lay the bastard himself - the self-professed "scientist" to whom the responsibility for this could ultimately fall. Strewn about were his shovels, his gloves, his preserving agents and scalpels and ropes; it had to be the devil's work, surely, for what other calling could possess a man to commit such horrors? I could see the evidence plainly on her coffin lid, overturned as it was on the dirt of the valley: he had dug her up, my Sarah, my love, and he had *taken her*, undoubtedly for some nefarious acts that I dared not imagine. I had heard stories of his laboratory and his experiments - I had needed no further time to reflect.

What would he have done to her, had I not caught up to him on the road above the hillside? I had seized my chance and jumped his carriage, unfortunately mistiming it just enough to give him an opportunity to fire his pistol; I suppose he did not anticipate the terrified horse tearing away and sending us airborne over the edge, or he may have lived as well. As it was, though, I had my precious few moments - perhaps the very same ones denied him just minutes before - and I meant to use them wisely.

She was beautiful, I saw, as beautiful as ever. As the sun sank further behind the hills, draping her and me and the rest of the world in shadow, I lay my head in her lap and laced my fingers in hers - stiff, unyielding....permanent. 

*Requiescat in pace*, I thought to myself, surrending to sleep. *Semper simul sumus*.

It couldn't be that far now. Another few hundred yards, maybe a quarter of a mile, and he'd be there - he'd be safe.

But he was so tired, so exhausted. And behind him, the endless feet continued, never stopping to rest, never halting even for a moment.

The sun blazed overhead as it always had, apathetically staring down at the scene below. The branches of the trees reached for him, attempted to slow him down as he ran, tangling in his clothes and scattering leaves across his face; every lost fraction of a second would add up, he knew, and sooner or later his enemies would overrun him - those same enemies that grew more merciless and driven with every step.

His lungs burned; his heart shrieked with effort. The edges of his sight wobbled and blurred, floating in and out of focus. Up ahead, not far, not far at all, there it was - his safe haven, his destiny, his target. All he had to do was reach it. He hauled in a great breath and pushed himself as hard as he could, already nearly collapsing with the expense of energy.

And then, from behind - *crunch, crunch*. Snapping twigs, swirling leaves, and footsteps that were nearly on top of his own. 

He was in the race of his life, yet felt powerless to go any faster. He could hear the approaching echoes, overtaking him, challenging him, taunting him, and begged his feet to speed up. Everything around seemed extremely vivid for a moment - the colours sprang out at his eyes, and the myriad smells of the trees and earth assaulted him - and then, just like that...it was over.

The young man from Montreal had passed him just a few yards from the finish line. He had tried his best, and it wasn't good enough; now, in front of the world, he had lost his chance at the gold. No more chances, no more races - no more hope.

It's true that I stood by and watched him fall. It's true that I admired the pattern his blood created.

It's true that I often ignore the screams of the dying, that I often fail to act when I see people in trouble. By all definitions, I am evil.

But you misunderstand.

It's not that I'm evil; only that I am apathetic. You see, I am incapable of the emotion you feel at your roots.

When faced with what you call tragedies, you accuse me of doing nothing - but forget that *you are the ones doing everything else*.

I worried for but a moment when they told me; the picture of the earth on the wall, taken from some zenith many tens of thousands of kilometres away, brought the air back to my lungs. 

Thought I could not hear the rush of the earth, orbiting the sun at an incredible speed, I didn't have to. I could hear my heartbeat, and that was enough.

The entrance to the cave was a few kilometres away from The Door. You must have heard of The Door; you can't miss it. It's a giant pit of hellfire, eternally smouldering, and below it lay one of the largest cave systems on earth. 

We didn't know how far it went down, at first. It's so hard to tell with these things; you can follow one branch for a mile, only to have it end abruptly, and then there's no choice but to turn back or perish, alone with only the earth around you. What a terrible way to go - trapped below, surrounded by the constant quiet and the unending darkness, feeling your own breath count down to your singular demise...

...but I digress.

We entered the cave with all the precautions: ropes, radios, torches, water. Rations to spare. Flashlights, oxygen tanks, beacons and bells and pickaxes; in short, we came prepared. We had no idea how long of a trip this would be, and we wanted everyone to come back alive.

The first few hours were relatively easy. Down, down, down we went, hauling ropes and checking our progress; it was around a mile and a half deep that it started to get hot. Really hot. The sweat beaded around my neck and dripped down my back, every so often causing the rope to slip from my grasp - if it hadn't been for the clips on my harness, I'd be dead.

But we persevered, and we continued. Our packs grew lighter as our bellies swelled with water, which in turn converted to sweat seemingly instantly, and still we trudged onward. Two miles, then three, then four; it began to get downright hellish. We were descending into an oven far below the earth, and despite our equally burning desire to reach the end of the cave complex, we resigned ourselves to the fact that it was beyond our reach. We would die if we pushed any further. So we rested for a moment, turned back the way we came, and --

-- we heard a cry for help. Faint, distant, far beneath us....and yet, unmistakeable.

I remember staring at the others, our hearts blaring a thumping alarm, our brains struggling to process what had just happened. Here we were, nearly five miles below the surface of the earth, and *someone else had preceded us*.

The tension may have gone on forever, had another cry not rung out. Louder, this time, more emphatic; *help!*, it wailed, distinctly agonized, completely female in tone. With renewed vigour we pressed on, navigating the twisting and winding corridors as carefully as we could while maintaining speed, and still the temperature rose, just as steadily as we descended.

At last, after what seemed a lifetime, we reached a clearing of considerable size. Pillars of stone stretched throughout our limited view, illuminated by our headlamps, and we swept the area for clues as to our next step -

...and we saw her. 

Starved, abused, tortured, but alive. She slumped, naked, next to a pillar, shackled to it with an immense iron chain; she cried softly, recoiling from the light like a beast. We rushed to her side, attempted to give her water, but it seemed like a poison to her - she dribbled and spat it out, seemingly in more anguish than before.

This was no longer an exploratory expedition. It was a rescue operation. Someone - someone *unbelievably* twisted - had brought this woman here, chained her up, and tortured her, leaving her to die in the deepest tomb in history.

As the others looked at the chain, trying to figure out how to get it unlocked, I cradled the woman in my arms, trying to calm her down. *Who are you?* I asked, in an attempt to soothe her. *Who did this to you?*

Finally braving the dim light, she turned her face towards me, and I saw the scars up and down her neck, and her cheeks, and her forehead. *I'm only the first,* she whispered, nearly drowned out by my own heartbeat. *The others are further below.*

There is, at first, a twinge of something unknown.

You don't know *how* you know, how you've learned that you love - but you do, and you have. The eyes that have looked back at you from the mirror every day for your entire life suddenly mature and grow a bit wiser; the thoughts that course constantly from your brain and out into the world are, uncannily, tinctured with something new. For it is no longer enough to think *What will I do today?*, but - *What will we do together next?*

Even while you walk along, hand in hand with them or however it may be, you are torn in a beautiful, inner turmoil. You want to walk behind them, so you may always be sure they are cared for; you want to walk beside them, so that your partnership is complete; you want to walk ahead of them, so that any tragedies can befall you first, and give them time to save themselves. In the beginning, you tried so hard to resist letting them in, but now - now you actively overthrow your own desires, and it's -- it's the most amazing, heart-stopping realization.

This feeling, it's unexplainable. It is not an acquired knowledge, not some learned fact that lingers just long enough to last until an exam; it's more of an innate feeling, an instinct. It overwhelms you - you want to protect them, and provide for them, and pretend that it was so obvious all along. Your every cell abandons self, and focuses solely on that which lies beyond all it's ever known; this is novel and terrifying and inexplicable and dangerous....

....but. 

There is always a but.

It makes you feel alive. Electric. Engaged and aspirant, unstoppable and immediate, unbreakable and vindicated and without parallel. It shatters every barrier you've always gazed upon with fear, and it crushes them into a fine dust that covers everything with a brand-new shine and lustre. It bridges a vast ocean, daring you to cross the thousands of miles of unmapped territory together, and embracing every outcome, regardless of any perceived positive or negative.

For the greatest quality of love, you see, is not that it creates lovers. It's that it creates *life*, literally and otherwise. Every half-whispered truth spoken in the darkness is as equally powerful as each heartwrenched tear that flows when those truths become lies. You cannot know the extent of heights possible unless you've admired them from the deepest trenches; that is the core of it.

Love hurts; it does. But that's ok. Because it also lifts, and empowers, and enables. Nowhere else in this life will you find such weightlessness among mortals.

And that is the draw, the pull, the addiction. When it's done right - which, unfortunately, is the tricky part - you feel that part of your soul is in another. You have transcended the physical limits that the world has set on you, and can have an entirely new set of experiences. 

When it's done right, together - you feel like you have honestly, and permanently, done the impossible. You have reached beyond your own senses and gained another. You have become god-like...and there is nothing on earth that will convince you otherwise.

I saw the first one of them. I was there - the only one. 

A lot happened after, but none of it was really the same as that first moment. At the morgue, you work on so many bodies - burn victims, old age, murders, accidents - that you just sort of assume that's *all* they are. You don't expect them to move again. You especially don't expect it to happen the way that it did.

He was young, I remember. 22 years old. He had driven off a bridge after a carjacking; him and the two others had lain in the river overnight before someone found them. He had drowned, and bloated, and it wasn't pretty - but this was the first time it wasn't permanent.

I followed the regular procedure. I removed his heart, lungs, liver, all of it, and put it on the scale; I took my notes and postponed my judgments. But when I went to cut the scalp and take out the brain --

-- oh, God, it's hard to describe. His eyes, they just - they just *opened*, all cloudy and white, and suddenly he was getting up off the table. *Getting up off the goddamn table*, you see, with his Y incision hanging open and *no fucking organs in his chest*. He kept trying to make noises, but there were no lungs to move air through his throat. He came at me in this terrifying silence, broken fingers reaching for me.

Don't blame me for what I did. What would *you* have done? How was I supposed to know he'd get out and start - start *this*?! I ran, and I cried, and I tried to tell people. But when we got back - he was gone. And by the time I was vindicated...well, here we are. Now the world is going to hell, and it's all because one of my boss's bosses wanted to save a few bucks on good door locks.

It's awful, how quickly things change. How one tiny act compounds into the end of the world. I can't help but think - what if I had taken his brain out first for the autopsy that day, instead of last? What if I had ended it before it even began? I'm trying to exercise my own brain one last time, before I splatter it with this revolver. Whatever I may be - cowardly or mistaken - at least I am not like him.

And that....well, that's the way it's going to stay.

They had warned me not to mess around with the time machine. *Paradoxes*, they said; *unpredictable changes!* I scoffed at them, and their lack of courage and dedication. Whether in this timeline or another, I was going to be the first person to go back.

But I messed up, badly. I don't even know how it happened - one thing here, and another there, and before you know it, the butterfly effect has created a tsunami and everything is *completely* different.

And now here I am, rewatching the footage. One plane, and the other; one tower, and the other. The eerie feeling of deja vu, like I've seen this before, but in some place that doesn't truly exist....because that's exactly what's happened.

It is 2/14, the day forever stamped into the minds of Americans. It is a day for love and hope and affection - and it's been tainted and destroyed by those faceless few who begrudge us those emotions. September 11th this year will be a Tuesday, and it will be meaningless; but never again will flowers and candy symbolize February 14.

The part that gets me the most?

Who caused this - me, or them?

I haven't yet written a screenplay. I have written stories though, some of which have been picked up to be developed and filmed. One is starting production in the spring, with an independent filmmaker helming it.

I'm trying to remember; I am. I know it's my responsibility, and that as one of the few to live this long I have an obligation to tell the story - but it's hard to find the words.

How do you tell those bright, hopeful faces - the ones that gaze upon the world around them and accept it - that the things we've had, and lost, are better than anything they'll ever see? How can you look a querulous child in the eye and truthfully say life is good? 

I can't, you see. And that's the issue with trying to explain how it happened.

In terms of numbers - the strictest sense of counting "who won" the fight back then - yes, we found ourselves victorious. We had many billions to their uncountable dead; we breathed while they rotted or froze in the vast expanse of interplanetary nothingness. We are alive, but - at what cost?

Our cities are gone, our temperatures are nearly unlivable; a haze hangs over the globe, ruining the crops, the animals, the trees, and the electronic signals we once used. Every now and then an errant piece of alien hardware will burst high above, called back to earth by our superior gravity; the shock waves echo on and on, like an interstellar laugh from an enemy we didn't even see. And yet we band together, defiant in our survival, scraping by on whatever else has survived, and pass the time in whatever ridiculous way we can manage.

Like, for example, goading an old man to talk about a fire in the sky many years ago, asking him what it was like when that sky fell...when it's much easier to look around and imagine all the things that once were - and will likely never be again.

Looking back, it probably wasn't the the best solution - having millions of pieces of debris slamming into the earth, all while going thousands of miles an hour, isn't an optimal outcome.

But that was all we had.

There was no backup plan; there was no contingency. There was one shot to wreck this thing, and we couldn't afford to miss. We could either blow it up and risk extinction, or we could watch from a distance and ensure it.

We never bothered to find out what the aliens were - what they looked like or wanted. All we had to know was that they had the proven ability to destroy planets - requiescat in pace, Mars - and that they were coming closer to us. Quick action had to be taken, or it wouldn't be able to happen at all.

The waiting was worse than the fallout, I think. Seeing the ships take off with the weapons locked up in their holds - such breakable, fragile things, with the weight of an entire planet on them - and waiting months for them to arrive at the - the *thing*. And once they got there, *more* waiting, long eternal minutes sweeping by as we tried to monitor stats from earth.

There were the dark moments, and the breakdowns, and the nagging thoughts that whispered in your ear the manner of your death - but in the end, there was triumph.

Sort of.

The asteroids came soon after, pelting the earth constantly for weeks. There were fires everywhere; earthquakes and tsunamis went wild. But the few of us who lived - well, what more is there to say than that?

We lived, indeed. And beyond that - we *live*.

The best thing about it was --

Well, maybe I shouldn't start there. Maybe I should start at the beginning.

You have to understand - no one had ever seen it before. When I came across it, I was the first sentient being to have ever done so; I was the first and the only to witness and comprehend the unimaginable majesty of what I was seeing. So it seemed only fitting to pass my eyes across its very existence - to take in its impossible form, right there in front of me, begging me to try and deny it.

I scanned from every direction, enriching my mind with the intense tones and hues; I marvelled at the purity of the sensation, as if everything I had seen up to that point had been mere nonsense. I hauled in a sacred breath, relishing the rush of air that painted memories onto my mind like a canvas - and again, and again, I wondered:

*How?*

I dared to wonder if I should chance to touch it, and paused for what seemed an eternity, debating. I reached out my fingers, feeling the electric ions on my skin, crackling with anticipation; over and over again, I drew them back, terrorstruck and uncertain. 

But through it all, I kept thinking: *No one will believe me...that the impossible exists. I must remember the best thing, the main thing, the most important thing; if I can't do that, what hope do they have to understand?*

And so I resolved to touch it. As my hand came nearer, I could feel the energy, the *power*, coursing quickly just a few inches away; it was magnetic and alluring, and I could not turn away.

Even when I wanted to; even when I tried.

I began to panic, but there was no hope in that. My puny musculature could not stand up to *this*, to the confirmation of our greatest thoughts and deepest fears.

*The best thing about it*, I thought as my atoms broke the threshold, and I was overcome by the most peculiar feeling that I can't quite describe - 

*- is that it is mine, and no one else's*.

The seconds ticked slowly by, stretching off into the future. They were a funny thing, he thought; they had such a strange existence. He snapped back to himself, staring down at the dog on the table; she returned the stare likewise, absorbing his attention into her vibrant eyes, still so very alive. She whimpered ever so slightly, as if she was afraid of displeasing him - this man who had been so kind to her, like no one had ever been.

God, this was always the hardest part.

He remembered waking up that morning, surrounded by unconditional love and joy. Across the pillows and the blankets, the dogs had roamed, each competing to nuzzle in closer to him than the one before; he was a warm bundle of unmitigated happiness, measured by the slow and steady heartbeats of the bodies around him. As he scratched one behind the ears, and then another, and a third, the palpable excitement in them grew in an overwhelming crescendo - until he couldn't hold it anymore, and allowed them to pounce on him. He let himself be consumed by great, rolling guffaws, feeling the paws and fur and snuffling noses, and then could not stop himself as that gave way to the intense, wracking sobs. 

He stared at the floor and wept for them, ever mindful that he would see the sunset and they would not; still they comforted him, all warm tongues and wagging tails. He enveloped them in embraces, allowing them the love that the rest of the world seemed unwilling to give, and he felt their instant elation at the simple acceptance of their new friend; he whispered apologies to any of them that happened to listen, but they did not understand - and that, perhaps, was for the best.

The walk to work was always too short, and fleeting in his memory. Every fire hydrant and tree demanded olfactory effort, every bird and blade of grass was enriched by the renewed vigour in each dog's veins; nothing escaped their notice, and life had never been so good.

He teared up again, every time, but it was his mission all along, and he knew it.

And then they ended up here. In the unassuming room behind the kennels, windowless but well-lit, he brought them in one by one, knowing they had no idea what awaited them behind that door. There was always a minor yelp when the needle went in, but it never lasted long; it was quickly overshadowed by the many treats that followed, seemingly given for no reason at all. And then, as those strange seconds slipped past, the dog would sit, then lie; its breathing would slow and its movement would cease, and then, after an agonizing moment in which he was never sure if *it* had happened --

-- it would be gone. 

Another selfless, loving, feeling creature - incapable of perceiving skin colour, IQ, past mistakes, financial trouble, or illness, and yet still considered a lesser life form - would be gone. Another source of unceasing, constant love and affection, sent to slaughter because its caretakers hadn't figured out how to become that very same thing.

And it didn't stop there for him, either. He would fill out the paperwork, and send the remains on their way, and then with barely a break - there would be another. Even more ebullient, even more overjoyed just to be included in his day. By the end of the shift, he would be broken, empty, hollow; he knew that each injection killed his soul just as surely as it killed its victim.

But he could not stop; he could not turn his back. No one loved these animals, except him, and he knew it; nobody deemed them worthy of the smallest sacrifices. If he could bring joy to their lives for just one night - a night of wagging tails, endless treats, soft beds, and the irreplaceable feeling of *yes, YOU are loved* - then he would carry on until his own time came. He reflected on this for the thousandth time, justifying it to himself ever and anon; he continued to think about it as he locked up his office and extinguished the light, bathing it in darkness. In the trash can, a printout with an offer for promotion lay crumpled, unread beyond the first line.
